title: Undoing Changes: Restore, Reset & Revert
description: Safely discard working tree edits, unstage files, adjust branch pointers with reset, and reverse public commits with revert.

blocks.content:
## Undoing Local Edits with `git restore`

Git 2.23 introduced `git restore` as a dedicated, safe command to undo uncommitted changes without touching commit history:

```bash
# Discard changes in a working directory file (reverts to last staged or committed state)
git restore app.py

# Unstage a file while preserving your edits in the working directory
git restore --staged app.py

# Discard all unstaged changes across the entire repository
git restore .
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SA["Staging Area (Index)"] -->|"git restore --staged <file>"| WT["Working Directory (Modified)"]
    HEAD["HEAD (Last Commit)"] -->|"git restore <file>"| WT
```

## Moving Branch Pointers with `git reset`

`git reset` moves the current branch pointer backward to an earlier commit. It has three primary modes:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph ResetModes [Git Reset Modes]
        Soft["--soft: Moves HEAD only. Staging and Working Tree stay intact."]
        Mixed["--mixed (default): Moves HEAD and updates Staging. Working Tree intact."]
        Hard["--hard: Moves HEAD, updates Staging, and overwrites Working Tree. Destructive!"]
    end
```

| Command | Updates HEAD? | Updates Staging Index? | Updates Working Tree? |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `git reset --soft HEAD~1` | Yes | No | No |
| `git reset --mixed HEAD~1` | Yes | Yes | No |
| `git reset --hard HEAD~1` | Yes | Yes | Yes (Data Loss Possible) |

> Warning: Never use `git reset --hard` if you have uncommitted working work you want to keep. It discards uncommitted changes permanently.

## Undoing Shared Commits with `git revert`

If you have already pushed a commit to a shared remote repository, rewriting history with `git reset` will break your teammates' branches. Instead, use `git revert`:

```bash
git revert 8f2c3d
```

`git revert` does not erase the bad commit. It creates a brand-new commit that applies the exact inverse diff:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C1["Commit 1: Add API"] --> C2["Commit 2: Buggy auth logic"] --> C3["Commit 3: Revert 'Buggy auth logic'"]
```

Because `git revert` only appends new history, it is completely safe for public, collaborative branches.

blocks.question: Which command removes a file from the staging area while leaving edits intact in your working directory?
blocks.explanation: 'git restore --staged <file>' copies the version from HEAD back into the staging area, unstaging the file without discarding your local file edits.

blocks.question: Why is 'git revert' preferred over 'git reset' for commits that have already been pushed to a shared remote branch?
options: git revert runs faster than git reset
git revert avoids rewriting history by appending an inverse commit, preventing conflicts for collaborators
git revert automatically resolves syntax errors in the compiler
git reset cannot be executed in Git terminals
blocks.explanation: Resetting changes past history, causing branch divergence and sync conflicts for teammates. Revert preserves history by adding a new commit that undoes the unwanted change.
